10.1029/WR005i002p00321.abstract: <jats:p>A variety of geophysical records are examined to determine the dependence upon the lag <jats:italic>s</jats:italic> of a quantity called ‘rescaled range,’ denoted by <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>t</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>s</jats:italic>)/<jats:italic>S</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>t</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>s</jats:italic>). If there had been no appreciable dependence between two values of the record at very distant points in time, the ratio <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>/<jats:italic>S</jats:italic> would have been proportional to <jats:italic>s</jats:italic><jats:sup>0.5</jats:sup>. But, in fact, as first noted by Edwin Hurst, the <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>/<jats:italic>S</jats:italic> ratio of hydrological and other geophysical records is proportional to <jats:italic>s<jats:sup>H</jats:sup></jats:italic> with <jats:italic>H</jats:italic> ≠ 0.5. Hurst's original claims must be tightened and hedged, and his estimates of <jats:italic>H</jats:italic> must be discarded, but his general idea will be shown to be correct. We have shown elsewhere that this behavior of <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>/<jats:italic>S</jats:italic> means that the strength of long‐range statistical dependence in geophysical records is considerable.</jats:p>
title: Some long‐run properties of geophysical records
